input: Turning to the question of pressure drop, it is interesting to note that the picture presented by the literature is far from settled, and two groups working in this area report pressure drop values for the same class of material that are, quite frankly, difficult to reconcile with one another. Each set of results appears to be internally consistent and carefully obtained, and yet the two sets simply do not agree, which raises some important questions about what is actually being measured. Part of the difficulty is that pressure drop across a bed of the benchmark material is not really a property of the material in isolation; rather, it depends on how the bed has been packed and on the basis on which the gas flow has been stated, as well as on the condition of the feed, and the two reports differ in precisely these respects. A set of values measured on a loosely settled bed and a set measured on a consolidated bed are, in a very real sense, measurements of two different beds. It is also worth mentioning that IAST comes into the comparison only indirectly, through the loadings that the groups report alongside their pressure drop data, and it has nothing to say about the pressure drop itself, so the discrepancy would remain even if everyone agreed on the adsorption side of things. On balance, the most sensible reading is probably a conditional one: where the design case in question resembles one group's test conditions, that group's values are the ones to use, whereas where it resembles neither set of conditions, the honest position is that the benchmark material does not yet have a pressure drop measured for the duty in question.
target: Two groups report pressure drop values for the same material class, and the values conflict: each set, taken on its own terms, is consistent, and the sets do not agree. The disagreement is not resolved by counting papers or by averaging the sets, because the sets were not measured in the same way. Pressure drop across a bed of the benchmark material is a property of the bed as packed and of the gas as supplied, not of the material alone, and the reports differ on exactly those points: the packing of the bed, the basis on which the gas flow is stated, and the condition of the feed. A set measured on a loosely settled bed and a set measured on a consolidated bed are measurements of two different beds, and the conflict between them is in part a conflict of conditions. IAST enters the comparison only through the loadings the groups report alongside their pressure drops, and it defines nothing about the pressure drop itself; the discrepancy survives any agreement on the adsorption side. The preference the evidence supports is limited and rests on a stated condition. Where a design case resembles one group's test conditions (the packing and flow basis of the intended bed), that group's values govern, because they were measured on a bed of that kind. Where the design case resembles neither, neither set governs, and the benchmark material still lacks a pressure drop measured for the duty in question.
